{{Short description|Formula about X-ray emission spectra}}
{{about|X-ray emission spectra}}

'''Kramers' law''' is a formula for the spectral distribution of [[X-rays]] produced by an [[electron]] hitting a solid target. The formula concerns only [[bremsstrahlung]] radiation, not the element specific [[X-ray fluorescence|characteristic radiation]]. It is named after its discoverer, the Dutch physicist [[Hendrik Anthony Kramers]].<ref name="kramers">{{cite journal|title=On the theory of X-ray absorption and of the continuous X-ray spectrum | last=Kramers|first=H.A.|date=1923|journal=Phil. Mag.|volume=46|pages=836|doi=10.1080/14786442308565244}}</ref>

The formula for Kramers' law is usually given as the distribution of intensity (photon count) <math>I</math> against the [[wavelength]] <math>\lambda</math> of the emitted radiation:<ref name="laguitton">{{cite journal| doi=10.1002/xrs.1300060409| last=Laguitton|first=Daniel|author2=William Parrish |date=1977|title=Experimental Spectral Distribution versus Kramers' Law for Quantitative X-ray Fluorescence by the Fundamental Parameters Method|journal=X-Ray Spectrometry| volume=6|issue=4|pages=201|bibcode=1977XRS.....6..201L}}</ref>
<math display="block">I(\lambda)d\lambda = K \left( \frac{\lambda}{\lambda_\text{min}} - 1 \right) \frac{1}{\lambda^2} d\lambda</math>

The constant ''K'' is proportional to the [[atomic number]] of the target element, and <math>\lambda_\text{min}</math> is the minimum wavelength given by the [[Duane–Hunt law]]. The maximum intensity is <math>\frac{K}{4\lambda_\text{min}^2}</math> at <math>2 \lambda_\text{min}</math>. 

The intensity described above is a particle flux and not an energy flux as can be seen by the fact that the integral over values from <math>\lambda_{min}</math> to <math>\infty</math> is infinite. However, the
integral of the energy flux is finite.

To obtain a simple expression for the energy flux, first change variables from <math>\lambda</math> (the wavelength) to <math>\omega</math> (the angular frequency) using <math>\lambda = 2\pi c/\omega</math> and also using <math>\tilde I(\omega) = I(\lambda) \frac{-d\lambda}{d\omega}</math>. Now <math>\tilde I(\omega)</math> is that quantity which is integrated over <math>\omega</math> from 0 to <math>\omega_\text{max}</math> to get the total number (still infinite) of photons, where <math>\omega_\text{max} = 2\pi c / \lambda_\text{min}</math>:
<math display="block">\tilde I(\omega) = \frac{K}{2\pi c} \left( \frac{\omega_\text{max}}{\omega} - 1\right)</math>

The energy flux, which we will call <math>\psi(\omega)</math> (but which may also be referred to as the "intensity" in conflict with the above name of <math>I(\lambda)</math>) is obtained by multiplying the above <math>\tilde I</math> by the energy <math>\hbar\omega</math>:
<math display="block">\psi(\omega) = \frac{K}{2\pi c}(\hbar\omega_\text{max}-\hbar\omega)</math>
for <math>\omega \le \omega_\text{max}</math>
<math display="block">\psi(\omega)=0</math>
for <math>\omega\ge \omega_\text{max}</math>.

It is a linear function that is zero at the maximum energy <math>\hbar\omega_\text{max}</math>.
